title: Refactoring in small safe steps
idea: Refactoring is changing code's structure without changing its behaviour, done as a chain of tiny named steps with the tests run after each one.
points: Characterization tests pin today's behaviour, quirks included, before you touch legacy code.
Take one named step, such as Rename or Extract Method, then run tests.
Green after every step means any failure points at the last small edit.
Never mix refactoring and behaviour changes in one commit; reviewers cannot separate them.

hero.title: Six safe steps on a legacy invoice

items.label: Pin behaviour
items.text: Write characterization tests for today's output, including the odd VIP boundary at exactly 1000.

items.label: Rename
items.text: Turn `c`, `q` and `t` into real names. Run the tests: still green.

items.label: Extract Method
items.text: Move the discount rule into `total()`. Run the tests: still green.

items.label: Parameter Object
items.text: Replace three parallel arrays with a `Line` record. Update test calls, run them.

items.label: Swap concatenation
items.text: Build text with `StringBuilder` instead of string `+=` in a loop. Run the tests.

items.label: Commit each step
items.text: Each green step is its own commit, so any one can be reverted alone.

code.title: Pin it first
code.caption: Legacy code wrapped in characterization tests before a single line of it changes.

walk.text: The legacy method: parallel arrays, one-letter names, pricing and formatting tangled together.
A characterization test records the exact text the code produces now, not what it should produce.
This pins a quirk: a VIP at exactly 1000 gets no discount. Keep it until someone decides.
The rule behind that quirk is `>` not `>=`. Refactoring must preserve it.
No JUnit here, so `check` prints PASS or FAIL. All three must pass before step one.

code.title: After the steps
code.caption: Same three tests, same expected text, all green. Only the structure changed.

walk.text: Introduce Parameter Object: one `Line` per item replaces three arrays that had to stay in sync.
`Invoice` validates its customer and copies the list, so callers cannot change it later.
Formatting only. `StringBuilder` replaces repeated string `+=` inside the loop.
Extract Method gave the pricing rule a name. The `>` boundary survived unchanged.
The expected strings are identical to before. Only the call shape changed with the new signature.

pitfalls: Fixing a quirk mid-refactor; pin it, finish, then change it in a separate tested commit.
Running tests only after a long rewrite; a failure then points nowhere useful.
Refactoring code with no tests; write characterization tests first, even crude ones.

quiz.q: Mid-refactor, you see a VIP at exactly 1000 gets no discount. It looks like a bug. What now?
options: Change > to >= now, while the code is open
Delete the boundary test because it pins a bug
Stop refactoring and rewrite the method from scratch
Keep the behaviour, finish refactoring, raise it separately
quiz.why: A refactoring must not change behaviour. Callers may rely on the quirk. Finish the structural steps green, then change behaviour in its own reviewed commit.

takeaway: Pin behaviour, take one small step, run tests, commit, repeat.

starters: How do I write characterization tests for code with no seams?
Which IDE refactorings are safe to run automatically?
